table.title: Distributed Systems Glossary
table.html:
TermDefinitionExample
IdempotencyProperty of an operation that produces the same observable result whether it is executed once or repeated with identical input, allowing safe retries after timeouts.A payment API accepts a client-supplied request key so a retried charge is not posted twice.
Eventual consistencyReplication model in which updates propagate asynchronously and replicas may temporarily disagree, but converge to the same state once writes stop and reconciliation completes.A user changes a profile photo; followers see it within seconds, though two regions may briefly show different versions.
BackpressureFlow-control mechanism by which a downstream consumer signals its capacity limits to an upstream producer, preventing unbounded queues, memory growth, and overload.A log shipper pauses reads when the indexing service reports its buffer above 80 percent.
Circuit breakerResilience pattern that monitors calls to a failing dependency and temporarily rejects requests after a threshold, giving the dependency time to recover instead of amplifying load.After five consecutive checkout timeouts, the client fails fast for 30 seconds before probing the service again.
QuorumMinimum number of replicas that must acknowledge a read or write for the operation to be considered valid, typically a majority in odd-sized clusters to avoid split-brain decisions.In a five-node cluster, a write succeeds after three nodes persist it and a read contacts three nodes.
Write-ahead logDurability technique in which changes are appended to a sequential log and flushed before being applied to the main data structure, enabling recovery after a crash.A database records each transaction in the WAL, then updates its B-tree pages during the next checkpoint.
CAP theoremTheorem stating that a distributed data store cannot simultaneously guarantee consistency, availability, and partition tolerance; during a network partition, designers must choose between consistency and availability.A payment ledger favors consistency and rejects writes when it cannot reach a majority of replicas.
table.brief: Glossary: term as row header (some long like "Eventual consistency"), definition (long), example (medium)

understanding.purpose: Explain distributed-systems terminology through definitions and illustrative examples.
understanding.reading: Readers scan the first column for a term, read across to understand it, and use the example to make the concept concrete; taller definition cells can absorb some wrapping in the other columns.
groups: Definition and Example are complementary explanatory prose columns; Term is the row identifier and scanning anchor.
keep_intact: Individual words and any identifiers within the text
Term labels where practical, especially multiword terms
may_wrap: Definitions and examples at natural word boundaries
Multiword term labels when a narrower term column makes more room for explanations

preferred.name: r2A
preferred.note: Shift 10px from Definition to Example to ease example wrapping while retaining the term width that keeps Write-ahead log together.

acceptable.name: r1B
acceptable.note: Preserve r0A's single-line term labels and move 20px from Definition to Example to improve the balance of prose within rows.

acceptable.name: r1C
acceptable.note: Test a middle ground between r0C and the more balanced alternatives: give definitions ample space while slightly widening both the term and example columns.

acceptable.name: r2B
acceptable.note: Give Example more room by narrowing Term slightly and Definition moderately; check whether the added example width improves row balance enough to justify any extra term wrapping.

acceptable.name: r2C
acceptable.note: Keep all term labels on one line while restoring 20px to Definition from Example; test whether the scanning benefit can coexist with acceptable example wrapping.

acceptable.name: r3A
acceptable.note: Restore the single-line Write-ahead log while keeping r2B's wider example column. Test whether a small reduction in definition width preserves its readable line breaks.

acceptable.name: r3B
acceptable.note: Keep the term column wide enough for Write-ahead log and give examples a little more room, testing whether their line endings improve without making definitions noticeably less comfortable.

acceptable.name: r3C
acceptable.note: Test the all-labels-intact approach with a more generous example column, taking space from definitions to see whether the two prose columns achieve a better balance.

bad.name: contrast
bad.note: The oversized term column leaves substantial unused space in most rows, while the narrow definition column forces long explanations into many short lines and makes the table harder to scan.
bad.why: The oversized term column leaves substantial unused space in most rows, while the narrow definition column forces long explanations into many short lines and makes the table harder to scan.

rationale: r2A gives definitions the most space while retaining a useful example column and a compact, easily scanned term column. Only one term wraps, and the longer definitions and examples generally occupy four or five lines without breaking words. The row boundaries keep each term, definition and example together, with a more balanced distribution of space than the wider-term alternatives.

general: Allocate width according to each column's role and content, while preserving enough space for row identifiers to be scanned.
Judge wrapping across whole rows: a shorter table is useful only when its text remains comfortable to read.
specific: Definitions need the largest share of this viewport, but examples also need enough width to read as short narratives.
Allowing 'Eventual consistency' to wrap frees space for both prose columns; keeping every term on one line makes the prose noticeably narrower.

tradeoffs: r2B is shorter and gives examples slightly more room, but also wraps 'Write-ahead log'. The wider-term designs keep every term on one line at the cost of narrower prose columns and taller rows.
uncertain: The ranges are conservative visual estimates, not browser-verified thresholds. A designer who prioritizes single-line row labels or more space for examples could reasonably choose a different candidate.

critique.good: Every term stays on one line, making the shaded first column easy to scan. Definitions have comfortable line lengths, and the headers are clear.
critique.problems: Examples repeatedly run to five short lines, leaving noticeable unused space beneath several definitions. The term column is spacious relative to its brief labels.
critique.cause: The 173px term column preserves the longest label but leaves only 196px for examples; the 350px definition column is more generous than the example column.

critique.good: Examples have comfortable line lengths, and most term labels remain intact. The two prose columns have a consistent visual weight.
critique.problems: Definitions become dense blocks of five or six lines, while shorter examples leave large blank areas in the same rows. Eventual consistency wraps, so the term column does not fully preserve the scanning advantage of r0A.
critique.cause: At 290px, Definition has nearly the same width as Example despite holding substantially more text. The 140px term column is too narrow for the longest label.

critique.good: The wide definition column gives the primary explanations an open, readable rhythm. Words remain intact, and the narrow term column returns useful space to the prose.
critique.problems: Three multiword terms wrap, interrupting the scan down the row identifiers. Examples still form narrow, often five-line blocks, leaving blank space beneath some definitions.
critique.cause: The 120px term column provides only 99px of text space, while the 199px example column is much narrower than the 400px definition column.

critique.good: The term column is easy to scan, with only Eventual consistency wrapping. Definitions and examples generally form balanced, readable row units, and words remain intact.
critique.problems: The longer examples wrap to five lines, leaving some definitions shorter than their accompanying examples. Eventual consistency occupies two lines.
critique.cause: The 219px Example column is relatively narrow; the 140px Term column is too narrow for the longest label.

critique.good: All term labels fit on one line, making the first column especially easy to scan. Examples remain readable and words stay intact.
critique.problems: Definitions wrap more heavily, producing several tall rows and a six-line CAP theorem definition. The generous term column leaves conspicuous empty space below short labels.
critique.cause: The 173px Term column uses width that the 330px Definition column could use more effectively.

critique.good: The 380px Definition column gives the primary explanations comfortable lines, and words remain intact.
critique.problems: Both Eventual consistency and Write-ahead log wrap. Examples become narrow and ragged; the Write-ahead log example takes five lines, increasing its row height despite the wider definition.
critique.cause: The 130px Term and 209px Example columns have both been compressed to give Definition 380px.

critique.good: The term column is easy to scan, and the definition has enough width to read comfortably. Write-ahead log stays on one line, and words remain intact.
critique.problems: The Circuit breaker example ends with an isolated 'again' and makes the row taller than its definition requires. Eventual consistency wraps, but remains easy to recognize.
critique.cause: The 229px example column falls just short of a useful line-break threshold; the 140px term column is too narrow for Eventual consistency.

critique.good: The 234px example column gives Circuit breaker a more balanced four-line example, improving the row rhythm. Definitions remain readable and no words split mid-word.
critique.problems: Write-ahead log wraps after the hyphen, making the term list less uniform and slightly harder to scan. Some definition lines still end with short fragments, especially 'overload.'
critique.cause: The 135px term column is just too narrow for Write-ahead log. The 350px definition column leaves Backpressure at five lines.

critique.good: All term labels fit on one line, making the first column especially easy to scan. The definition column retains the same readable measure as the other designs.
critique.problems: Examples feel cramped and frequently determine row height. Quorum ends with an isolated 'nodes.' and Write-ahead log ends with 'checkpoint.', leaving noticeable unused space beneath shorter definitions.
critique.cause: The 173px term column reserves enough room for the longest label but reduces the example column to 196px.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

contrast.why: Terms stay on one line, but the wide term column leaves considerable empty space while definitions wrap into five to seven lines.

r1C.why: The generous definition column makes the main explanations easy to read, though two terms wrap and the narrower examples sometimes run to five lines.

r2A.why: Definitions and examples have balanced, readable widths, and only one term wraps. The quorum definition breaks the hyphenated phrase odd-sized across lines.

r1B.why: All terms remain on one line, supporting quick lookup, while definitions and examples have enough room to read comfortably. The rows feel coherent despite some longer definitions.

ref_equal.why: All terms fit on one line, but the equal columns give the short labels excessive space and squeeze definitions into many short lines.

ref_auto.why: Definitions and examples are well proportioned and rows scan easily, though two term labels wrap, including Write-ahead log.

raw.unsure: C and F use the width efficiently; the preference for D depends on how much value the reader places on keeping every term on one line.

r1C.why: Definitions have comfortable line lengths and rows scan clearly, but the narrow term column wraps two labels and the examples are comparatively cramped.

ref_auto.why: Definition and example columns are well balanced, though two row labels wrap and the example for eventual consistency ends with a lone word.

contrast.why: All terms stay on one line, but the wide term column leaves substantial unused space while definitions wrap into tall blocks.

r1B.why: Every term stays on one line, while definitions and examples have useful, proportionate widths. Rows remain easy to scan across despite some longer definition blocks.

ref_equal.why: Nearly equal columns give the short terms excessive space and squeeze the longer definitions into narrow, tall blocks, leaving large empty areas in the other columns.

r2A.why: The definition and example columns read comfortably and most terms remain intact, but eventual consistency wraps and some rows have uneven text depths.

raw.unsure: F is a close alternative if keeping definitions wider is more important than keeping every term on one line.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
